newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila's arrest of leftist a warning to APEC foes.
newsitem.headline: Manila's arrest of leftist a warning to APEC foes.

text.p: The Philippines has showed its determination to provide tight security for the APEC summit by arresting a leftist leader and threatening to take control of firms facing labour unrest, analysts said on Wednesday.

Filemon Lagman, chairman of a workers' group that the military has linked to alleged communist-inspired plots to disrupt the November 25 summit, was arrested on Tuesday while meeting with union officials in a hotel in Manila's suburbs.

Lagman's arrest, on charges of murdering a policeman in 1992, coincided with strike threats by unions in the hotel, transport and telecommunications sectors that will provide key services to the summit and the ministerial meeting preceding it.
Manila newspapers have said supposed plans against the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit by leftist groups include fomenting strikes among workers in those sectors.
"The state has other measures, like taking over vital industries," Justice Secretary Teofisto Guingona told reporters, referring to government options to counter the strike threats.

Despite government denials that Lagman's arrest was linked to APEC security preparations, many political analysts said it was a warning to leftists that the military would not tolerate attempts to disrupt what President Fidel Ramos has called the country's biggest event this decade.
"The government is pulling all the stops to ensure security for APEC," said Alex Magno, a political science professor at the University of the Philippines.
But while the government may have a case against Lagman, the timing of his arrest was politically unwise, Magno said.
"What the government wants to do during the summit is to advertise the democratic space we have so the arrest of Lagman would undermine that message..." he said.
But Magno added that the government appeared ready to absorb the political costs of Lagman's arrest.

Labour disputes have been simmering in vital firms such as the national air carrier Philippine Airlines (PAL), where flight attendants have held protest rallies over pay after ground crews last month went on a three-day strike over the same demand.

Among other establishments threatened with walkouts is the country's premier Manila Hotel, where U.S. President Bill Clinton and Indonesian President Suharto are to stay when they arrive for the APEC summit at nearby Subic Bay.
"It's a warning shot across the bow of the demonstrators, that they can't get too far," political analyst Teodoro Benigno said of Lagman's arrest.
"I think the government would like to find out what the reaction would be in the ranks of the protesters, whether the arrest would cool them off," Benigno added.
If arresting Lagman did not curb anti-APEC protests by leftist and other groups, the government would probably crack down more, he said.

The leftist BMP (Coalition of Filipino Workers), which Lagman heads, is one of several private groups organising four separate conferences opposed to the APEC goal of full scale regional trade and investment liberalisation.
BMP and two other groups plan to end their anti-APEC meetings with motorcades to Subic Bay on the day of the summit.
At least 30,000 workers have been mobilised to join the protest, BMP officials have said. Police said they would block any attempt by the protesters to get near the summit venue.
